title: Voice- / gesture-controlled robot
desc: A Teachable Machine model drives an Arduino robot — an AI × Arduino crossover
content_html:
Materials

  • 1 x Arduino Uno R3 (Nerokas, nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x L298N Dual H-Bridge Motor Driver Module (Nerokas, nerokas.co.ke)
  • 2 x DC Gear Motors with wheels (Pixel Electronics, pixelelectronics.co.ke)
  • 1 x Caster/support wheel (Pixel Electronics, pixelelectronics.co.ke)
  • 1 x Robot chassis plate (acrylic or plywood, two-layer or single-layer) (Pixel Electronics, pixelelectronics.co.ke)
  • 1 x Battery pack — 4xAA holder with switch or 7.4V Li-ion pack (Nerokas, nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x Jumper wire pack (Male-Male and Male-Female) (Nerokas, nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x USB cable (Type A to Type B, for Uno) (Nerokas, nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x Small breadboard (optional, for prototyping connections) (Nerokas, nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x Laptop with Google Chrome browser and a working webcam and/or microphone (school/student-provided)
  • Screws, double-sided tape, or zip ties for mounting components to chassis
  • Small screwdriver set

How It Works

This project connects two worlds: a "thinking" AI model running on a laptop, and a "doing" robot built from Arduino. Think of it like a translator standing between a brain and a body.

First, we use a free website called Teachable Machine to train a mini AI brain. We show it pictures from a webcam (like a hand pointing left, right, or a "stop" fist) or we let it listen to spoken words ("forward", "stop"), and we tell it which class each example belongs to. After seeing enough examples, the model learns to recognise new, unseen gestures or sounds and guess which class they belong to — this is called a prediction.

The Teachable Machine model runs entirely inside the Chrome browser using JavaScript — it never touches the Arduino directly. So we add a small bridge: whenever the browser is confident about a prediction (say, "left" with high confidence), it sends a single letter like L down the USB cable using something called the Web Serial API — this lets a Chrome browser tab talk to a device plugged into a USB port, just like the Arduino Serial Monitor does.

The Arduino is running a simple sketch that constantly listens on its Serial port. When it receives a letter, it looks it up (F = forward, B = backward, L = left, R = right, S = stop) and sends the matching electrical signals to the L298N motor driver, which is powerful enough to actually spin the two DC motors — something the Arduino's own pins cannot do alone. The motors turn, and the robot moves — all because of a hand gesture or spoken word the AI recognised a second earlier.

Step-by-Step Instructions

  1. Assemble the robot chassis: attach the two DC gear motors to the base plate, fit the wheels, and add the caster wheel at the front or back for balance.
  2. Mount the L298N motor driver and Arduino Uno onto the chassis using tape or screws, leaving the USB port accessible.
  3. Wire the motors to the L298N: left motor to OUT1/OUT2, right motor to OUT3/OUT4.
  4. Wire the L298N to the Arduino: ENA→pin 5, IN1→pin 8, IN2→pin 9, ENB→pin 6, IN3→pin 10, IN4→pin 11. Connect L298N GND to Arduino GND (common ground is essential).
  5. Connect the battery pack's positive and negative leads to the L298N's 12V and GND screw terminals. Do not power the motors from the Arduino's 5V pin — it cannot supply enough current.
  6. Upload the Arduino sketch (below) to the Uno using the USB cable. Open the Serial Monitor, set baud rate to 9600, and type F, B, L, R, S to confirm the robot responds correctly to each letter before continuing.
  7. On the laptop, open teachablemachine.withgoogle.com in Chrome and start a new Image Project (for gestures) or Audio Project (for voice commands).
  8. Create classes matching the robot's commands, e.g. Forward, Backward, Left, Right, Stop. Record at least 30-50 samples per class using the webcam or microphone, varying angle/lighting/tone slightly so the model generalises well.
  9. Click Train Model and wait for training to finish. Test each class live in the Preview panel and confirm predictions are accurate; retrain with more samples for any class the model confuses often.
  10. Export the model: choose Tensorflow.js, click Export, and either use the provided sample code or open the hosted "Export" project link. Add the Web Serial connection code (provided in the Full Code section) to the exported sketch.js so predictions above a chosen confidence threshold are converted into single-letter serial commands.
  11. Close the Arduino Serial Monitor (Chrome cannot access the COM port if it is already open elsewhere), then open the modified Teachable Machine web page in Chrome and click the "Connect to Arduino" button, selecting the correct COM port from the pop-up list.
  12. Test each gesture or spoken command in front of the webcam/microphone and observe the robot moving accordingly. Discuss with students why there is a small delay between doing the gesture and the robot responding.
  13. Fine-tune the confidence threshold and the COMMAND_TIMEOUT safety value in the Arduino sketch so the robot stops promptly when no gesture is being shown.

Full Code

// Voice/Gesture Controlled Robot - Arduino Receiver Sketch
// This sketch waits for single-character commands sent from the
// Teachable Machine web page (via USB Serial, using the Web Serial API)
// and drives two DC motors through an L298N motor driver accordingly.

// ---- Motor driver pin definitions ----
const int ENA = 5;   // Enable pin for left motor (PWM speed control)
const int IN1 = 8;   // Left motor direction pin 1
const int IN2 = 9;   // Left motor direction pin 2
const int ENB = 6;   // Enable pin for right motor (PWM speed control)
const int IN3 = 10;  // Right motor direction pin 1
const int IN4 = 11;  // Right motor direction pin 2

const int MOTOR_SPEED = 180; // 0-255 PWM value - adjust for your motors/battery voltage

char lastCommand = 'S';           // Remembers the last command received
unsigned long lastCommandTime = 0; // Tim
